2022_231_2022_bod_elections_booklet.page:
**What it is**
Candidate information booklet for the 2022 Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Board of Directors elections, supplied to the Troy School District Board of Education. It reprints MASB Bylaws Article IV, Section 2 on active membership, explains the balloting procedure, and prints statements from ten candidates.

**Membership structure (Bylaws Article IV, Section 2)**
Active members are divided into eight regions drawn on intermediate school district boundaries: Region 1 (Copper Country, Delta-Schoolcraft, Dickinson-Iron, Eastern Upper Peninsula, Gogebic-Ontonagon, Marquette-Alger RESA, Menominee County); Region 2 (Alpena-Montmorency-Alcona ESD, Charlevoix-Emmet, Cheboygan-Otsego-Presque Isle ESD, COOR, Iosco RESA, Manistee, Northwest Education Services, Wexford-Missaukee); Region 3 (Ionia County, Kent, Mecosta-Osceola, Montcalm Area, Muskegon Area, Newaygo County RESA, Ottawa Area, West Shore ESD); Region 4 (Bay-Arenac, Clare-Gladwin RESD, Clinton County RESA, Gratiot-Isabella RESD, Midland County ESA, Saginaw, Shiawassee RESD); Region 5 (Genesee, Huron, Lapeer County, Sanilac, St. Clair County RESA, Tuscola); Region 6 (Allegan Area ESA, Barry, Berrien RESA, Branch, Calhoun, Heritage Southwest, Kalamazoo RESA, St. Joseph County, Van Buren); Region 7 (Eaton RESA, Hillsdale County, Ingham, Jackson County, Lenawee, Livingston ESA, Monroe County, Washtenaw); Region 8 (Macomb ISD, Oakland Schools, Wayne RESA).

Members are also grouped by pupil membership:

| Group | Pupil membership |
| --- | --- |
| I | All intermediate districts |
| II | 0 - 1,400 |
| III | 1,401 - 2,500 |
| IV | 2,501 - 5,000 |
| V | 5,001 - 11,000 |
| VI | 11,001 - 40,000 |
| VII | more than 40,000 |

**Election mechanics**
Five seats are up. The MASB Board comprises 22 members including three at-large directors; sixteen directors are elected from the eight regions, two per region, plus one director each from Groups V, VI and VII. Article VIII, Section 6 permits only one director from any one local or intermediate school district board; Article VIII, Section 8 directs that unopposed nominations be declared elected without an election. Seats up are Regions 3, 4, 7, 8 and Group VI, each a three-year term. Region 3 continues with John Siemion, Ottawa Area ISD, and Group VI with Marc Siegler, Walled Lake Consolidated Schools, both unopposed with no ballots sent. Regions 4, 7 and 8 vote by online ballot. One ballot per district was emailed to the superintendent secretary of record on Jan. 28, 2022 and may not be forwarded; ballots must be submitted and confirmed by 1 p.m. Wednesday, March 2, 2022 in a two-step submit-then-confirm process. Unofficial results post to a voicemail recording at 517.327.5915, generally after 2 p.m. on the deadline date, and by email that afternoon; official results are approved at the March 18, 2022 Board of Directors meeting. No local district or ISD funds may be used for campaigning, including district email accounts; questions go to MASB Legal Counsel Brad Banasik, J.D. (bbanasik@masb.org, 517.327.5929) or Cheryl Huffman (517.327.5915, chuffman@masb.org).

**Candidates**

| Region | Candidate | District | Page |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | Phil Rausch | Midland Public Schools | 5 |
| 4 | John Tramontana | DeWitt Public Schools | 6 |
| 4 | Karen Uebler | Frankenmuth School District | 7 |
| 7 | Guillermo Lopez (incumbent) | Lansing School District | 8 |
| 7 | Susan Marlin-Zeilser | Monroe Public Schools | 9 |
| 7 | Michael McVey | Saline Area Schools | 10 |
| 8 | Melandie Hines | Wayne Westland Community Schools | 11 |
| 8 | Darlene Pomponio (incumbent) | Southgate Community Schools | 12 |
| 8 | Angie Smith | Farmington Public Schools | 13 |
| 8 | Michael Swiecki | Wyandotte Public Schools | 14 |

The booklet closes with the MASB mission statement: to provide high-quality educational leadership services for all Michigan boards of education and to advocate for an equitable and exceptional public education for all students.
2022_231_2022_bod_elections_booklet.verbose:
Candidate booklet for the 2022 Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Board of Directors elections, circulated to member boards including the Troy School District Board of Education. It contains three parts: an excerpt of the MASB Bylaws defining active membership, an explanation of the election and email voting procedures, and biographical pages with election statements from the ten candidates seeking seats in Regions 4, 7 and 8.

MEMBERSHIP STRUCTURE. MASB Bylaws Article IV, Membership, Section 2 (Active Members) provides that the board of education of any public school district in Michigan may become an active member, and that active members are divided into eight regions designated according to intermediate school district boundaries. Region 1: Copper Country ISD, Delta-Schoolcraft ISD, Dickinson-Iron ISD, Eastern Upper Peninsula ISD, Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD, Marquette-Alger RESA and Menominee County ISD. Region 2: Alpena-Montmorency-Alcona ESD, Charlevoix-Emmet ISD, Cheboygan-Otsego-Presque Isle ESD, COOR ISD, Iosco RESA, Manistee ISD, Northwest Education Services and Wexford-Missaukee ISD. Region 3: Ionia County ISD, Kent ISD, Mecosta-Osceola ISD, Montcalm Area ISD, Muskegon Area ISD, Newaygo County RESA, Ottawa Area ISD and West Shore ESD. Region 4: Bay-Arenac ISD, Clare-Gladwin RESD, Clinton County RESA, Gratiot-Isabella RESD, Midland County ESA, Saginaw ISD and Shiawassee RESD. Region 5: Genesee ISD, Huron ISD, Lapeer County ISD, Sanilac ISD, St. Clair County RESA and Tuscola ISD. Region 6: Allegan Area ESA, Barry ISD, Berrien RESA, Branch ISD, Calhoun ISD, Heritage Southwest ISD, Kalamazoo RESA, St. Joseph County ISD and Van Buren ISD. Region 7: Eaton RESA, Hillsdale County ISD, Ingham ISD, Jackson County ISD, Lenawee ISD, Livingston ESA, Monroe County ISD and Washtenaw ISD. Region 8: Macomb ISD, Oakland Schools and Wayne RESA. Active members are also divided into seven groups based on pupil membership: Group I, all intermediate districts; Group II, districts of 0 - 1,400 pupils; Group III, 1,401 - 2,500; Group IV, 2,501 - 5,000; Group V, 5,001 - 11,000; Group VI, 11,001 - 40,000; and Group VII, more than 40,000.

ELECTION PROCEDURE. Five seats on the MASB Board of Directors are up for election. The Board is comprised of 22 members, including three at-large directors. Sixteen directors are elected from the eight regions, two from each region, and one director per group is elected from Groups V, VI and VII. Directors are elected by active member school boards. The MASB President nominates a member to serve as an at-large director, subject to Board approval. Article VIII, Section 6 of the bylaws permits only one director to be elected or appointed from any one local or intermediate school district board. Article VIII, Section 8 provides that if any nomination is unopposed, the Board of Directors shall declare the unopposed candidate elected without conducting an election for that group or region. The seats up this year, one seat each and three-year terms unless otherwise noted, are Regions 3, 4, 7, 8 and Group VI. Region 3 will continue to be represented by John Siemion, Ottawa Area ISD, unopposed with no ballots sent; Group VI will be represented by Marc Siegler, Walled Lake Consolidated Schools, also unopposed with no ballots sent. Voting in Regions 4, 7 and 8 takes place by online ballot. No local district or ISD funds may be used to campaign for anyone running for a seat, a rule that prohibits candidates from using district email accounts to message other board members; personal email accounts must be used. Each district received one ballot, emailed to the superintendent secretary on record with MASB on Jan. 28, 2022, and ballots cannot be forwarded. Completed ballots must be submitted and confirmed by the superintendent secretary by 1 p.m. on Wednesday, March 2, 2022, in a two-step process: submit the ballot, then confirm it has been submitted. Unofficial results are available on a voicemail recording at 517.327.5915, generally after 2 p.m. on the deadline date, and by email that afternoon; official results will be approved at the March 18, 2022 Board of Directors meeting, which newly elected directors should plan to attend. Questions about campaign expenditures go to MASB Legal Counsel Brad Banasik, J.D., at bbanasik@masb.org or 517.327.5929; general questions to Cheryl Huffman at 517.327.5915 or chuffman@masb.org.

REGION 4 CANDIDATES (three-year term). Phil Rausch, Midland Public Schools, Midland County, three years on the board, offices held Vice President and Secretary, no MASB certifications listed. He states he is serving his fourth year on the Midland board, attended Midland Public Schools K-12 where his children now attend, and works as Solar Commercial Manager at Hemlock Semiconductor. His priorities are student achievement including skilled trades and vocational paths, student safety and mental health supports, and before- and after-care for dual-income and single-parent families. John Tramontana, DeWitt Public Schools, Clinton County, seven years on the board, offices held Secretary and Treasurer. He was hired as MASB's Director of Communications, PR and Marketing in 2014 and spent five years with the organization as employee, board member and CBA instructor. He serves on the board of the Michigan Society of Association Executives, chairs the American Society of Association Executives Communication Professionals Council, serves on the board of the Veterinary Medical Association Executives, and is Treasurer of the DeWitt board. Karen Uebler, Frankenmuth School District, Saginaw County, nine years on the board, offices held Vice President, Secretary and Treasurer; MASB certifications Certified Boardmember Award and Award of Merit. She cites the 1963 state constitution's guarantee of a free, quality, equitable public education, notes fifty-nine years have passed, describes Army service and use of the G.I. Bill to earn a bachelor's degree, and has served on her local board since 2013.

REGION 7 CANDIDATES (three-year term). Guillermo Lopez, Lansing School District, Ingham County, incumbent, 22 years on the board, offices held President and Treasurer; certifications Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit and Award of Distinction. A retired teacher, he names the COVID pandemic as the most important issue and pledges continued support for MASB's Diversity, Equity and Inclusion work and for training districts that cannot cover costs. Susan Marlin-Zeilser, Monroe Public Schools, Monroe County, one year on the board, no offices listed; certifications Certified Boardmember Award and Award of Merit. A teacher of almost seven years, former foster parent and permanent parent to three children, she cites staffing shortages, legislation undermining community districts, and mental health, behavioral and special education funding. She serves on the MASB Government Relations Committee, joined the Special Education Parent Action Committee of Monroe County ISD, was elected School Board Liaison to Monroe County ISD for fiscal year 2022, and is developing a forest school option. Michael McVey, Saline Area Schools, Washtenaw County, five years on the board, offices held Vice President and Secretary; certifications Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction, Master Boardmember Award, Master Diamond Award and Master Platinum Award. He reports more than 40 years serving students and schools, began as an English, Special Education and ESL teacher (in Japan), authored "Meeting the Internet Challenge," taught at the University of Arizona, earned a doctorate in Education, is a professor of Teacher Education at Eastern Michigan University, and served as President of the Washtenaw Association of School Boards (WASB).

REGION 8 CANDIDATES (three-year term). Melandie Hines, Wayne Westland Community Schools, Wayne County, seven years on the board, offices held Vice President and Secretary; certifications Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction and Master Boardmember Award. She served as Vice President for one year and Secretary for three years, and with a team of 10 people and community organizations passed a $158 million bond in 2018 across six communities: Wayne, Westland, Inkster, Romulus, Canton and Dearborn Heights. She sits on the Executive Board for the 13th Congressional District, the Policy Committee and the Career College Readiness Committee, belongs to Top Ladies of Distinction, advises Top Teens of America, and mentored for the Champions of Wayne Mentoring Program; she cites the "Portrait of a Graduate" model and a restructured K-12 curriculum adding STEAM and a virtual high school. Darlene Pomponio, Southgate Community School District, Wayne County, incumbent, 13 years on the board, offices held President, Vice President and Secretary; certifications through the President's Award, including Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction, Master Boardmember Award, Master Diamond Award and Master Platinum Award. She has held officer positions for the past 10 years, served WCASB as an executive board member for 11 years with an officer position for 10, participated in MASB's Resolutions and Bylaws and Government Relations committees over 11 years, and has served on the MASB Board of Directors for the last three years. Her degrees include a Bachelor of Science in Criminal Justice, an MBA in Strategic Management and a PhD in Applied Management and Decision Sciences, plus Teacher and School Administrator Certification for Michigan. Angie Smith, Farmington Public Schools, Oakland County, six years on the board, office held Secretary; certifications Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction and Master Boardmember Award. She was employed at Detroit Public Schools in special education and has served as Building PTA President, PTA Council president, PTA State Region D Representative and Co-Chair of the Farmington/Farmington Hills MCMR MLK Walk. Michael Swiecki, Wyandotte Public Schools, Wayne County, 28 years on the board, offices held Vice President, Secretary and Treasurer; certifications Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction, Master Boardmember Award, Master Diamond Award and Master Platinum Award. He has had two children graduate from Wyandotte Schools and four grandchildren attend, expects to be seated on the WCASB Executive Board at its next meeting, and is working on the President's Award Level.

The booklet closes with the MASB mission statement: to provide high-quality educational leadership services for all Michigan boards of education, and to advocate for an equitable and exceptional public education for all students.

2022_232_final_2022_2023_soc_recommendat.paragraph: Administrative recommendation for the Troy School District's Schools of Choice program for 2022-2023, presented by Assistant Superintendents Kris Griffor (Elementary Instruction) and Christine DiPilato (Secondary Instruction) in a memorandum dated February 15, 2022. Using Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projections and a sibling survey of current SOC families, administration recommends accepting applications for 18 Kindergarten, 3 First Grade and 16 Middle School students, with the option to admit more in the third week of August if space allows. Supporting data show 285 SOC students against 4847 non-SOC students in the elementary buildings, or 5.55%, concentrated most heavily at Hill Elementary at 19.72%.
2022_232_final_2022_2023_soc_recommendat.page:
**What it is**
Administrative presentation and accompanying memorandum recommending the Troy School District's Schools of Choice (SOC) participation for the 2022-2023 school year, prepared by Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, and Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction. The memo is dated February 15, 2022 and addressed to the TSD Board of Education.

**Program framing**

Recommendation package for the Troy School District's Schools of Choice (SOC) program for the 2022-2023 school year, comprising a slide presentation and a memorandum dated February 15, 2022 to the TSD Board of Education from Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, and Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction. The presentation opens by defining Schools of Choice as a program that provides non-resident students with additional enrollment opportunities, notes that participation is optional for districts, and states that the degree and extent of participation, including application enrollment dates, grade levels and building assignment, are determined at the local level.

ELEMENTARY ENROLLMENT PROJECTIONS. Projections submitted by Plante Moran Cresa compare "Most Likely" figures against actual counts for kindergarten and first grade. For 2019/2020 the kindergarten most likely was 835 against an actual of 838, and first grade most likely 891 against an actual of 888. For 2020/2021 the kindergarten most likely was 844 against an actual of 761 as of 1/28/21, and first grade most likely 884 against an actual of 829 as of 1/28/21. MEMORANDUM AND RECOMMENDATION. 2022_233_mental_health_supports_020122.paragraph: Presentation on Troy School District mental health supports, describing how school counselors, school psychologists and school social workers together form a system of support for students and the school community. It catalogs each discipline's current responsibilities across consultation, evaluation, crisis response and MTSS Tiers 1 through 3, describes Student Assistance Team membership and SRSS screening completed four times per year at secondary and three times per year at elementary, and presents a November staff module on anxiety citing that 7.1% of children (4.4 million) ages 3-17 have a diagnosed anxiety disorder and that 80% of children who have anxiety do not get help.
2022_233_mental_health_supports_020122.page:
**What it is**
Presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education titled "Mental Health Supports - School Counselors, Psychologists and Social Work: creating a system of support for students and the school community," describing the current roles of each of the three support disciplines, the district's tiered structures, and a sample staff professional development module on anxiety.

**School counselors - current state**
Consultation and therapeutic intervention duties include individual therapeutic intervention; crisis intervention at the individual, familial and building level; threat assessment for suicidal ideation; the referral process; coordination with in-patient and out-patient therapists; social emotional support during disciplinary hearings; 9th grade interactive SEL classes; therapy dogs; restorative practices; At-Risk/SRSS/SEL/MTSS work; participation in SST; and teacher and staff mental wellbeing support. Events include 9-12 class meetings, 8th grade student and parent presentations, junior college-planning and testing presentations, College Night, Honors Convocation, graduation, college visits and a financial aid evening. Caseload duties include college planning meetings with every senior, individual scheduling for every student, two weeks of schedule changes at each semester start, enrollment and placement testing, AP test coordination, Common Application letters of recommendation, National Merit Semi-Finalist and Presidential Scholars applications, OSTC, 504 referrals, IEP annual meetings, 21F, NCAA, virtual at-home and foreign exchange students, scholarships, newsletter, military, Weebly/Twitter/Instagram, and the Seal of Bi-Literacy.

**School psychologists - current state**
Support struggling and diverse learners, academic achievement, positive behavior and mental health, safe learning environments, school-family-community partnerships and school-wide data-based decision making. Duties span consultation, REED and evaluation (CA-60 review, classroom consult, data analysis, REED and Prior Written Notice development, formal assessments, facilitating initial MET/IEP meetings) and pre-referral work across Tier 1 (needs assessment, benchmarking, SRSS data mining, SEL training, PBIS), Tier 2 (short-term direct intervention, systematic observation, progress data, P2P) and Tier 3 (executive coaching, Functional Behavior Assessments and PBIS plans, staff training). They also maintain CPI certification and serve on the building Key Identified Personnel (KIP) team.

**School social workers - current state**
Carry IEP or Section 504 caseloads, conduct eligibility evaluations, maintain service records and progress monitoring, handle Medicaid documentation and billing, lead Functional Behavior Assessments and Positive Behavioral Intervention Support Plans, train HCA/staff, monitor discipline and facilitate MDR, serve as KIP leader, and connect families to community resources. Tiered work runs from schoolwide SEL training, Zones of Regulation and bi-weekly principal meetings on SEL data, through Tier 2 check-in/check-out and four to six week small-group or 1:1 instruction, to Tier 3 eight to twelve week intensive instruction and crisis response including CPS referral.

**Structures**
Student Assistance Teams at elementary include the teacher consultant, school psychologist, school social worker, speech language pathologist, ELD, literacy specialist, math interventionist, principal and general education teacher; secondary teams include the school psychologist, school social worker, speech and language pathologist, special education teachers, counselors, assistant principal and principal. The SRSS screener is completed four times per year at secondary (at semester) and three times per year at elementary, providing one piece of data for building teams.

**Staff capacity building - anxiety module (November SEL series)**
Cited statistics: 7.1% of children (4.4 million) ages 3-17 have a diagnosed anxiety disorder; 32% of adolescents are estimated to have anxiety in the United States; 80% of children who have anxiety do not get help; higher levels are seen in females; among children diagnosed with anxiety, 1 in 3 will have a behavioral problem, and among children with behavior issues, 1 in 3 will be anxious. Sources include the American Psychological Association, NIMH, CDC and Jessica Minahan.

**Next steps**
Continue developing district and building structures, establish community partnerships, build capacity and understanding around mental health, strengthen connections for students, enhance social emotional learning in all buildings, develop crisis response training, and continue identifying needs in Tiers 1, 2 and 3.
2022_233_mental_health_supports_020122.verbose:
Board presentation titled "Mental Health Supports - School Counselors, Psychologists and Social Work: creating a system of support for students and the school community," delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on February 1, 2022. It inventories the current responsibilities of each of the three student-support disciplines, describes the district's tiered systems and team structures, presents a sample staff professional development module on anxiety, and lists next steps.

SCHOOL COUNSELORS - CURRENT STATE. Under consultation and therapeutic intervention, counselors provide individual therapeutic intervention; crisis intervention at the individual, familial and building level; threat assessment for suicidal ideation; the referral process; coordination and communication with in-patient and out-patient therapists; collaboration with administration; social emotional support during disciplinary hearings; 9th grade interactive SEL classes; therapy dogs; restorative practices with administration; At-Risk, SRSS, SEL and MTSS work with all students; participation in SST; staff meeting presentations on SEL support and crisis intervention support; and teacher and staff mental wellbeing support. Under events and presentations, counselors run 9, 10, 11 and 12 grade class meetings; 8th grade student presentations and meetings at all middle schools; an 8th grade parent evening presentation with Q&A; junior presentations for college planning and standardized testing; College Night; the Honors Convocation evening event; graduation; college visits; and a financial aid evening event. Caseload responsibilities include management of an individual caseload; an individual college planning meeting with every senior student; individual scheduling for every student; schedule changes for two weeks at the start of semester 1 and semester 2; enrollment of new students and placement testing; AP test coordination; college applications including the Common Application with letters of recommendation for all seniors; National Merit Semi-Finalist applications; Presidential Scholars applications; OSTC; 504 referrals and management of all 504s at the middle school level; IEP annual meetings; 21F; NCAA; virtual at-home students; foreign exchange students; scholarships; the newsletter; military; website and social media via Weebly, Twitter and Instagram; and the Seal of Bi-Literacy.

SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGISTS - CURRENT STATE. School psychologists support struggling and diverse learners, academic achievement, positive behavior and mental health, safe and supportive learning environments, school-family-community partnerships, and school-wide data-based decision making. Their consultation, REED and evaluation work includes collaborating with local district administrators and school-based leadership teams on MTSS activities, participating in problem-solving teams requiring knowledge of data collection and analysis, curriculum-based assessments and tiered systems of interventions; comprehensive review of the CA-60; general education classroom consultation; data collection and analysis; supporting staff in identifying and using research-based instructional practices; attending grade level and special education data review meetings and secondary department meetings; working with the building principal and/or interventionist or department leads to select a grade level or department to support; REED and Prior Written Notice (PWN) development; formal assessments as directed by the REED; and scheduling initial IEPs, creating the initial invitation and facilitating MET/IEP meetings. Pre-referral duties are organized in tiers. At Tier 1 psychologists may perform a building needs assessment, assist in benchmarking to establish baseline data for at-risk students, help mine SRSS data and take an active role in problem solving, provide consultation and support for Tier 1 at-risk classes and students at the secondary level, deliver SEL training for all staff, and support classroom and building implementation of universal supports and PBIS. At Tier 2 they provide short-term direct intervention in areas of identified need, recommend classroom interventions for at-risk students, collect data during systematic observations, maintain current performance data documenting progress and intervention effectiveness with re-evaluation as needed, may assist with a P2P partner, and may be assigned as an intervention partner to determine next steps. At Tier 3 they may function as an executive coach, assist with Functional Behavior Assessments and PBIS plan development, assist with training teachers, teams and support staff in Tier 3 interventions, collaborate with the behavior support team, and conduct follow-up observations and meetings. Additional responsibilities include providing professional learning and consultative services to local educational staff upon request, establishing and attending departmental professional learning, case study collaboration, maintaining CPI certification, participating on the building Key Identified Personnel (KIP) team, building capacity and consistency in school psychologists' practices, and sensitivity training for student-specific needs.

SCHOOL SOCIAL WORKERS - CURRENT STATE. Social workers carry an IEP or Section 504 caseload and are active MTSS participants and team members. Duties include providing direct or consultative services through needs identified in the IEP or 504 process; collaborating on IEP development; conducting evaluations to determine or re-determine eligibility and service needs; maintaining service records and progress monitoring; Medicaid documentation and billing; serving as team leader for Functional Behavior Assessments and Positive Behavioral Intervention Support Plans; collaborating with outside therapists and support services; providing community resources and direct support to families; training HCAs and staff on PBIS plan implementation; monitoring discipline and facilitating MDR; serving as Key Identified Personnel (KIP) leader; sensitivity training for student-specific needs; and working with general education teachers on student needs and interventions. Tier 1 schoolwide work includes serving as KIP team member and leader for all students, building team member for student, staff and family crisis and trauma intervention, attending SSW discipline meetings and building meetings to collaborate on SEL, attending special education department meetings, collaborating with families and outside therapists or agencies, providing community resources, leading professional development on tiered socio-emotional and behavioral supports, scheduling bi-weekly meetings with the building principal to review schoolwide and student-specific SEL data, supporting any student in immediate crisis or danger such as through the safety protocol for suicide or self-injurious behavior, facilitating and educating on CPS referral, delivering SEL training for all staff, supporting universal supports implementation, reviewing SRSS data, collaborating on the school improvement team including PBIS implementation, implementing Zones of Regulation, and push-in whole group lessons one to three times. Tier 2 work includes collaborating with general education teachers interested in P2P, working on classroom-wide PBIS systems, joining grade level meetings when SEL data is discussed, leading development of Tier 2 PBIS plans such as check-in/check-out and token systems, Zones of Regulation Tier 2 support, serving as a P2P partner, identifying data collection systems, targeted push-in whole group short-term general education lessons such as executive functioning, short-term four to six week small-group or 1:1 instruction with skill-specific data collection, and observation and follow-up to determine next steps. Tier 3 work includes Zones of Regulation Tier 3 support, check-ins for students who identify as being in the "red zone" during daily reporting, team leadership for Functional Behavior Assessments and PBIS plan development, Peer to Peer leadership, training teachers, teams and support staff in Tier 3 interventions, collaboration with the behavior support team, longer-term eight to twelve week intensive small-group or 1:1 instruction, parent communication, and follow-up observation and meetings.

UNIQUE SKILLS. School counselors are distinguished by individualized therapeutic intervention, secondary and post-secondary academic counseling and planning, standardized testing coordination, large group developmental interventions, threat assessment, and vocational and career development. School psychologists focus on child development from birth through 26 years of age, individual behavior, academic and ability assessment, and consultation, data analysis and problem solving at the systems, building, classroom and individual level. School social workers focus on identification of students at risk, early intervention, problem solving services to students, parent interactions, school personnel, behavioral intervention and student crisis response, and involvement with community agencies.

TEAM STRUCTURES AND SCREENING. Elementary Student Assistance Team members are the teacher consultant, school psychologist, school social worker, speech language pathologist, ELD, literacy specialist, math interventionist, principal and general education teacher. Secondary team members are the school psychologist, school social worker, speech and language pathologist, special education teachers, counselors, assistant principal and principal. Secondary buildings complete the SRSS screener four times per year, at semester, and elementary buildings complete it three times per year; SRSS provides one piece of data for building teams to review when determining student social-emotional needs. Staff capacity is built through monthly presentations on topics intended to simultaneously build understanding and capacity across the district.

ANXIETY MODULE (SEL PRESENTATION SERIES, NOVEMBER). The sample module reports that 7.1% of children (4.4 million) ages 3-17 have a diagnosed anxiety disorder, that 32% of adolescents are estimated to have anxiety in the United States, that 80% of children who have anxiety do not get help, that higher levels of anxiety are seen in females, that among children diagnosed with anxiety 1 in 3 will have a behavioral problem, and that among children who have issues with behavior 1 in 3 will be anxious. Signs in the school setting include difficulty concentrating, distraction, forgetfulness, difficulty shifting attention between tasks, inattentiveness, negative behavior change, changed peer or adult relationships, poor academic performance, difficulty initiating tasks, appearing unmotivated, lazy or uninterested, perfectionism, school avoidance or refusal, social withdrawal, increased complaining, clinginess, negative thoughts, fear of failure or embarrassment, and rigid or inflexible thinking. Anxiety is described as impairing intake of new information and long-term memory, executive functioning such as planning and working memory, social interactions including group work and presenting, perspective-taking and transitions, and as creating all-or-nothing thinking. Teacher guidance under "Put Your Oxygen Mask on First" covers setting literal or metaphorical boundaries, self-validation, expanding one's social support "village" because social support increases resilience, self-care beyond bubble baths, and modeling non-anxious coping by tolerating uncertainty, focusing on the here and now and being genuine. Listed resources include anxietyintheclassroom.org, a School Resources Wakelet, gozen.com, the MGH PRIDE learning management course, a Feeling Thermometer by Aureen Wagner, PhD, and mindfulschools.org. Sources cited are the American Psychological Association, the National Institute of Mental Health, the CDC's children's mental health data pages, anxietyintheclassroom.org and Jessica Minahan.

NEXT STEPS. Continue to develop structures at the district and building levels; establish community partnerships; continue to build capacity and understanding around mental health; strengthen connections for students; enhance social emotional learning in all buildings; develop crisis response training; and continue to identify needs in Tiers 1, 2 and 3.
